questions.q: In the worked budget, why is the output reserve subtracted first, before anything else?
options: Output tokens are free and don't count toward the window
A response cut off mid-answer because input used up nearly the whole window is a worse failure than a slightly smaller input budget
The system prompt must always be smaller than the output
Models refuse to generate output unless it's budgeted first
questions.explain: Reserving output first avoids the worse failure mode of a truncated response, so it's set aside before input budgeting begins.

questions.q: What distinguishes a 'fixed cost' from a 'variable cost' in a context budget?
options: Fixed costs are always larger than variable costs
Variable costs don't count against the token limit
There is no real difference between the two
Fixed costs (system prompt, tool schemas) don't change call to call; variable costs (history, retrieval) grow and need an explicit cap
questions.explain: Fixed costs are constant and measured once; variable costs grow over time and must be capped or they eventually consume the whole budget.

questions.q: Using the rule of thumb (~0.75 words per token), roughly how many tokens is a 3,000-word document?
options: About 4,000 tokens
About 400 tokens
About 750 tokens
About 12,000 tokens
questions.explain: 3,000 words / 0.75 words-per-token ≈ 4,000 tokens, matching the worked example in the lesson.

questions.q: What does the lesson identify as the most common way a context budget quietly breaks?
options: Setting the output reserve too high
Measuring the system prompt's token count incorrectly
Leaving history or retrieval uncapped, so one of them eventually consumes the whole remaining budget
Using too many tool schemas
questions.explain: Without explicit caps on variable components like history and retrieval, either one can grow unchecked and crowd out the rest of the budget.

questions.q: According to the lesson, why should code or non-English text get extra token padding in an estimate?
options: Because they are not supported by context windows at all
Because they tend to tokenize less efficiently per character than plain English prose
Because tool schemas are always written in code
Because the output reserve must be doubled for code
questions.explain: The ~4-characters-per-token rule of thumb is calibrated for English prose; code and non-English text typically use more tokens per character.
